content: Systemic circulation refers to the part of the cardiovascular system responsible for transporting oxygenated blood from the heart to the rest of the body and returning deoxygenated blood back to the heart. This process is distinct from pulmonary circulation, which involves the exchange of gases in the lungs. In systemic circulation, arteries carry oxygen-rich blood to the tissues. As blood flows through the body, oxygen diffuses from the blood into the cells surrounding the capillaries, while carbon dioxide diffuses from the cells into the blood. Veins then transport the deoxygenated blood back to the heart. Oxygenated blood enters systemic circulation as it exits the left ventricle of the heart through the aortic semilunar valve. The first major vessel in this pathway is the aorta, a large and thick-walled artery. The aorta arches and branches off to supply the upper body before passing through the diaphragm to deliver blood to the lower body via its various branches. Blood flows from arteries into capillaries, which are the smallest and most numerous blood vessels. These capillaries connect tissues to arterioles and facilitate the delivery of oxygen and nutrients to cells. Peripheral tissues do not completely deoxygenate the blood, so venous blood still contains oxygen, albeit at a lower concentration than arterial blood. Additionally, carbon dioxide and metabolic waste products are added to the blood at this stage. Deoxygenated blood is collected by venules, which then drain into veins. The blood eventually flows into the inferior and superior venae cavae, which return it to the right atrium of the heart, completing the systemic circulation cycle. The blood is then re-oxygenated in the pulmonary circulation before re-entering systemic circulation. The venous system collects relatively deoxygenated blood, which converges into two major veins: the superior vena cava (draining areas above the heart) and the inferior vena cava (draining areas below the heart). These two large vessels empty into the right atrium of the heart, marking the end of systemic circulation. Additionally, the coronary sinus drains the veins of the heart itself into the right atrium. One significant advantage of systemic circulation, powered by the muscular left ventricle, is the ability to deliver oxygenated blood at high pressure to all parts of the body simultaneously. This is in contrast to open circulatory systems or the gill-based systems used by fish, which are less efficient in distributing oxygenated blood.
